title: The Dyatlov Pass Incident: Why Did 9 Hikers Run Into the Snow?
subject: dyatlov
description:
What do you think drove them out of the tent? 👇

In February 1959, nine experienced hikers left their tent on a frozen slope in the northern Ural Mountains, in the middle of the night, without their boots. This case file follows the search, the investigation, the theories and the 2021 avalanche study that finally offered an answer — and the questions it still leaves open.

Sources: Communications Earth & Environment (Gaume & Puzrin, 2021); EPFL; Wikipedia, "Dyatlov Pass incident" and its references.

thumbnail.text: THEY CUT THE TENT FROM INSIDE

scenes.text: On the twenty-sixth of February, 1959, a search party climbed a frozen slope in the northern Ural Mountains and found a tent.
It was half collapsed and buried in snow. Boots, coats and food were still inside. And the canvas had been cut open, from the inside.
Leading away from it, down the mountain, were footprints. Nine sets. Some in socks. Some in a single shoe. Some barefoot.
The nine people who made them had walked into the dark, at night, in temperatures far below freezing, and none of them ever came back.
The investigators who studied the case in 1959 would close it with a vague phrase. Decades later, prosecutors and scientists would still be arguing about what really happened on that slope.
For more than sixty years, this has been one of the strangest cases in modern history. Tonight, we open the file.
The group came from the Ural Polytechnic Institute in Sverdlovsk, the city known today as Yekaterinburg. Most were students or recent graduates, and all were experienced in winter hiking.
Their leader was Igor Dyatlov, a twenty-three-year-old radio engineering student. The oldest member was Semyon Zolotaryov, a thirty-eight-year-old war veteran and instructor.
Their goal was Otorten, a mountain far in the north. It was a demanding route, rated the hardest category of the time, and they planned to cover it on skis.
Their cameras and diaries were later recovered. The photographs show an ordinary, cheerful trip: young people on skis, posing in the snow, laughing around the stove at night.
On the twenty-seventh of January, they left Vizhai, the last inhabited settlement on the way. The next day, one of them turned back.
Yuri Yudin was suffering from knee and joint pain. He said goodbye to his friends and returned home. He would be the only one of the ten who lived.
The remaining nine pushed on. On the first of February, with daylight fading, they made camp on the open slope of a mountain the local Mansi people called Kholat Syakhl.

It was an unusual choice. A sheltering forest lay about a kilometre and a half below. Yudin later suggested that Dyatlov did not want to lose the height they had gained, or wanted practice camping on an open slope.
Whatever the reason, they dug a flat platform into the snow, pitched their long canvas tent, and settled in for the night.
They expected to send a telegram from Vizhai by the twelfth of February. That telegram never came.
At first, nobody worried. Delays were normal on long winter routes. But by the twentieth of February, the families were demanding a rescue, and the first search teams set out.
Students and volunteers joined the search, then soldiers, aircraft and local Mansi hunters who knew the land better than anyone.
Six days later, they found the tent. Investigators concluded that it had been cut open from the inside, as if the hikers could not wait to get out through the entrance.
They followed the footprints for about a kilometre and a half down the slope, to the edge of a forest. There, under a tall Siberian pine, they found the remains of a small fire.
Beside it lay Yuri Doroshenko and Yuri Krivonishenko, dressed only in their underwear.

Between the pine and the tent, three more were found, spread out along the slope: Igor Dyatlov, Zinaida Kolmogorova and Rustem Slobodin. Their positions suggested they had been trying to climb back toward the tent.
Five of the nine were found. Four were still missing, and the snow was deep. The search would go on for months.
On the fourth of May, as the snow began to melt, searchers found the last four, in a ravine about seventy-five metres from the pine, under four metres of snow.
They were Lyudmila Dubinina, Semyon Zolotaryov, Alexander Kolevatov and Nikolai Thibeaux-Brignolles. Some of them were wearing clothes that belonged to the friends found by the fire.
This is where the case turned from tragic to strange. Six of the nine had died of hypothermia. But three of the four in the ravine had severe injuries.
One had a major skull fracture. Two had serious chest fractures. The forensic examiner compared the force to that of a car crash, yet there were few outward marks on their bodies.
And there was one more detail. Tests on some of the clothing found traces of radiation.

To the families, none of it made sense. These were careful, experienced people. Leaving a tent without boots, at night, in that cold, was something none of them would have done without a very good reason.
In May 1959, the investigation was closed. The official cause of death was a compelling natural force. The files were sent to a secret archive.
With no clear answer, the theories began. The first suspicion fell on the local Mansi people, but investigators found no sign of a struggle and no tracks other than the hikers' own.
Some believed the group had stumbled into a secret military test. That idea grew from the radiation traces and from reports of strange lights in the sky that winter.
Decades later, the original investigator, Lev Ivanov, said that he had been ordered to keep parts of the case quiet, and that he believed bright flying spheres had played a role.
Others pointed to the weather. A katabatic wind, a sudden, violent blast of cold air pouring down a mountain, could have made staying in the tent feel impossible.
Another idea was infrasound, a low-frequency sound produced by wind around a mountain, which some people say can cause panic. There is little evidence that it played a role.
And then there was the oldest theory of all, an avalanche. For decades, many experts dismissed it. The slope was not steep, and searchers saw no clear avalanche debris.
It was the simplest explanation, and for a long time it seemed to explain the least.
In 2019, Russian prosecutors reopened the case. The following year, they announced their conclusion: an avalanche, combined with poor visibility.
Then, in January 2021, two scientists, Johan Gaume of the Swiss institute EPFL and Alexander Puzrin of ETH Zurich, published a study that took the idea seriously.
They suggested that the hikers' own camp had weakened the slope. To pitch the tent, they had cut into the snow. Then strong winds piled more snow above them through the night.
Hours later, a small slab of packed snow could have broken loose and pressed down on the tent. Not a huge avalanche, but enough to cause crushing injuries to anyone lying beneath it.
To test it, the researchers used computer models, including animation software developed for the film Frozen, and data from car crash studies.

Critics had long argued that the slope was too gentle for an avalanche, and that searchers saw no clear debris. The researchers replied that a small slab could leave little trace once the wind had covered it again.
If they are right, the hikers cut their way out to escape a slope they believed was about to bury them, and headed for the shelter of the trees.
But the study does not explain everything, and the researchers themselves say so. The radiation, the strange lights and the hikers' last hours remain open questions.
Today, the place where they died is called Dyatlov Pass. Nine people walked into the dark there, and more than sixty years later, we still do not know exactly why.
Yuri Yudin, the one who turned back, spent the rest of his life asking what had happened to his friends. He died in 2013, still without a full answer.
